body_markdown:
Imagine tackling a crusty loaf of sourdough with scissors. Sounds like a cumbersome, frustrating process that’s unlikely to yield a good sandwich slice, right? You should use a nice, long serrated knife. Crisp cuts with minimal effort! See? The correct tool makes all the difference.


So how did I—like so many other millennial parents—end up buying a three-row SUV, when we all know that[no family vehicle beats a minivan](https://www.hagerty.com/media/new-car-reviews/after-all-these-years-the-chrysler-minivan-still-makes-sense-is-that-enough/) ?


Eric Weiner


My wife, Michelle, and I have a two-year-old daughter. For the last couple of years, our 2011 Toyota RAV4 V-6 worked fine as the household’s primary kid-hauler. But with another child on the way, we recognized the need for more functional space and enhanced safety. Vehicles are perhaps the only area of my life where I can claim any authority or expertise, so I laid down the full-court press on the idea of adding a minivan to our fleet.


Eric Weiner


Michelle was receptive, to her credit. She grew up in the back of a Toyota Sienna (for me, it was a Chrysler Town & Country) and she conceded that a minivan was indeed the sensible choice. “I’ll test drive one,” she allowed. “But the thought of piling into a van in a parking lot, or seeing it in my spot in the garage, feels like giving up on ever being cool again.”


For most of us, nothing is as uncool as one’s parents. And our generation grew up riding in minivans. Dodge Caravans, Ford Windstars, Honda Odysseys—those were the chosen chariots for school drop-off, sports practice, and family vacations. Traffic today is thick with large SUVs, indicating how that tide has turned in the last quarter-century.


Eric Weiner


Sam Fiorani, vice president of global vehicle forecasting at AutoForecast Solutions, quantifies the minivan’s steady decline like this: “In the U.S. market, 1.37 million minivans were sold in 2000 when 19 different models were offered. Those numbers fell almost every year until hitting the bottom in 2020, when only 228,000 were sold.”


They weren’t sexy, but compared with the long station wagons of the prior era, minivans were triumphs of utility. Brilliant front-wheel-drive packaging? Check. Practical sliding doors, check. A deep cargo area behind the rear bumper, check. Configurable interior seating, which you can even remove for stress-free Home Depot visits, check-check.


Sienna Platinum


Toyota


Nevertheless, these days, only five minivans remain in production. Hordes of high-riding three-row SUVs have taken their place. Many of them look great—chunky, tough, and in some cases, hugely capable off-road. Their purposeful styling instills a sense of adventure, even if the trunk will more often be full of diapers and yogurt pouches than wetsuits and kayak paddles. “That new Toyota 4Runner looks beautiful,” Michelle declared one morning. “I’m going to test drive it.”


4Runner SR5


Toyota


Toyota


That she did, alongside a handful of other Toyotas (we’re dealing with a brand loyalist here). Her consideration list included the aforementioned 4Runner, as well as the Highlander, Grand Highlander, and Sienna. These were her notes from her visit to Germain Toyota of Dundee, Michigan:


- **4Runner:** “Looks amazing. But it’s so tall, I can’t easily climb into it. That would be annoying, not to mention trying to put kids into car seats. Pass.”
- **Highlander Hybrid:** “Really solid. I like how quiet it is and that it’s a hybrid. Not sure if it’s big enough, though. I don’t want to drive a monster truck, but the trunk seems a little small and the third row is basically useless.”
- **Grand Highlander Hybrid Max** : “Could be the one. It’s so nice inside. There’s a lot of space, but I still find it easy to drive. And the 360 camera makes me feel a lot more confident about parking something this big. And, yeah, it’s super fast. Even quicker than my V-6 RAV4! ?”
- **Sienna AWD:** “I get it. I want to want it. But it seems huge from behind the wheel, and I feel nothing when I drive it. Plus, it really drags a** compared with the Grand Highlander.”


You can probably guess what happened next: We placed an order for a black 2026 Grand Highlander Hybrid Max Platinum. With roof rails and running boards.


Can’t say I wasn’t disappointed, as the Sienna would have been my top choice. At the same time, I have three other cars. She should love her car as much as I do mine.


Eric Weiner


Eric Weiner


Eric Weiner


Eric Weiner


In the end, we’re both pretty thrilled with it. After thousands of miles of driving, between daycare drop-off and several extended road trips, I have to admit that I love the Grand Highlander, too. SUV or not, thanks to 400 lb-ft of torque, it’s punchy as hell and comfortable to pilot in day-to-day scenarios. The doors don’t slide, but the openings are huge, which makes toddler-loading pretty simple. We’ve had plenty of full-size adults in the third row, with nary a complaint.


Eric Weiner


SUVs will likely maintain market domination for the foreseeable future, but I was pleased to learn from Fiorani that minivans are clawing back. “There’s not a wholesale shift toward minivans, but they are gaining some market share,” he explained. “Before 2024, North American production of minivans was well under the 300,000-unit level. Starting in 2024, the Toyota Sienna and Chrysler Pacifica have grown in popularity, moving total production of the segment closer to 400,000 vehicles a year. Americans bought almost 126,000 Chrysler Pacificas, 101,000 Toyota Siennas, and 88,000 Honda Odysseys last year with growth expected this year. Kia will sell about 85,000 imported Carnival minivans this year, up from 72,000 last year and less than 50,000 in 2024.”


Eric Weiner


Diehard minivan dads and moms shouldn’t get all excited, though, Fiorani warns: “That long-standing but undeserved milquetoast reputation of minivans will keep them from returning to the segment’s earlier glory, and the production limitations will prevent significant growth in volume.”


The Great Unminivanning of the last 25 years is likely to remain the status quo. I had hoped I’d be able to escape the phenomenon’s clutches, but alas, marriage requires compromise. Fortunately, we won’t suffer for it. The Toyota is a gem, and family SUVs these days, in general, hew closer to the utility of minivans than ever before. Most important, Michelle loves it. She cried when we parted with her RAV4, but the sorrow soon passed, and driving the Grand Highlander brings her a lot of joy. It’s our serrated knife—the right tool for the job.
